procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 30, 1970, of the Jammu and Kashmir High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 12 of 1969 and Criminal Reference No. 10 of 1969, which dismissed the appellant's appeal and confirmed the sentence of death.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant was convicted of murder by the Sessions Court and sentenced to death. The case went to the High Court as a criminal appeal by the appellant and as a murder reference for confirmation of the death sentence. The High Court examined a ballistic expert and permitted the appellant to examine another ballistic expert (Siyaram Gupta) and two other witnesses (Shri Ratan Sahgal and C. L. Wasan). C. L. Wasan was allowed to be examined even though he had already been examined earlier as a prosecution witness. The High Court declined the appellant's request to produce more defense witnesses. Ultimately, the High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the death sentence. An oral prayer for a certificate to appeal to the Supreme Court was declined.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition after the High Court declined to grant a certificate to appeal. The Supreme Court granted special leave and heard the appeal. The Supreme Court focused on two points raised by the appellant's counsel, stating that if they agreed with the appellant on those points, the appeal would succeed and the appellant would be acquitted without considering other arguments about guilt. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court disregarded legal processes and failed to consider vital aspects, causing serious prejudice to the appellant, and that grave and substantial injustice appeared to have resulted from the infirmities in the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient legal evidence to prove that it was the appellant who fired the fatal shots.

facts: The appellant was convicted of murder by shooting, and the conviction was confirmed by the High Court.
The primary witness, who filed the First Information Report (F.I.R.), did not provide any description of the shooter in the report.
The witness also did not state in the F.I.R. that he knew the appellant beforehand.
No test identification parade was conducted to have witnesses identify the appellant prior to the trial.
The witness identified the appellant for the first time in the Sessions Court.
The High Court had relied on statements made by witnesses to the police during the investigation (under s. 161, Cr. P.C.) to corroborate their testimony in court.
law: The substantive evidence of a witness is their testimony given in court.
Statements made to the police during an investigation under s. 161, Cr. P.C. are not admissible as corroborative evidence at trial.

When an accused person is not previously known to a witness, an identification made for the first time in court, without a prior test identification parade and without corroborating details (like a description in the F.I.R.), is considered a very weak and slender piece of evidence.
application: The Supreme Court first ruled that the High Court was in error for relying on the statements made by witnesses to the police (under s. 161, Cr. P.C.) to support the conviction. The Supreme Court excluded these statements from its consideration.

The Court then scrutinized the evidence of the main witness who filed the F.I.R. It noted that his identification of the appellant in court was highly unreliable because he had failed to provide any description of the shooter in the F.I.R. and had never identified the appellant in a test parade.
The Court deemed the witness's in-court identification, standing alone, as "far too slender a piece of evidence to support the appellant's conviction."
The Court also found the testimony of other eyewitnesses to be untruthful and stated it was "wholly unable to place any reliance on the testimony of anyone of these witnesses."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that there was insufficient legal evidence to prove the appellant was the shooter. After excluding the inadmissible statements made to the police and finding the in-court identification evidence to be unreliable and weak due to the absence of a test identification parade and lack of description in the F.I.R., the Court found no reliable material on which the conviction could be sustained. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal and acquitted the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in using statements recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code during investigation for the purpose of corroborating the statements made by witnesses in court.

facts: The High Court had relied on statements made by witnesses to the police during the investigation, which were recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The purpose for which the High Court used these statements was to find corroboration for the testimony the same witnesses later gave in court.

Specifically, the High Court used the Section 161 statements to support the witnesses' in-court testimony that the accused's name had been disclosed to the police, a fact that was not mentioned in the initial First Information Report (F.I.R.).
law: The Supreme Court cited Section 162 of the Cr.P.C., which explicitly prohibits the use of statements made to the police during an investigation for any purpose at trial.
The only exception to this rule, as provided in the section, is that such statements can be used to contradict a witness in the manner provided by Section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act.
The Court emphasized that the language of Section 162 is "plain and explicit" and that it clearly prohibits using these statements for corroborating testimony in court.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's action was a direct violation of the prohibition laid down in Section 162 Cr.P.C.
The Court stated that the High Court was "clearly in error" for taking the contents of the Section 161 statements into consideration to corroborate the witnesses' court testimony.
The Court repeatedly pointed out this error, stating that the High Court had used the statements of a large number of witnesses for this impermissible purpose.
By excluding these improperly considered statements, the Supreme Court found there was no reliable legal evidence left on the record to sustain the conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court had committed a clear legal error. According to Section 162 of the Cr.P.C., statements recorded by the police during an investigation cannot be used to corroborate a witness's testimony in court; their use is strictly limited to contradicting the witness. Because the High Court wrongly used these statements for corroboration, its decision was overturned, and the appellant was acquitted.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient legal evidence to prove that it was the appellant who fired the fatal shots.
appellant_arguments: Although some eyewitnesses claimed in court to have heard the appellant's name being called out at the scene, neither his name nor this fact was mentioned in the First Information Report (FIR).
If the appellant's name was truly disclosed to the authorities immediately after the incident, steps would have been taken to arrest him right away, but no such action was taken.
No test identification parade was conducted to establish the identity of the assailant.
respondent_arguments: The omission of the appellant's name in the FIR is not a serious enough discrepancy to cast doubt on the prosecution's case.
The FIR was lodged immediately after the occurrence, and the failure to mention the name was an omission of a 'minute detail'.
The eyewitnesses had clearly stated the appellant's name in their statements to the police (under Section 161 Cr.P.C.) shortly after the FIR was lodged, which supports their testimony in court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in using statements recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code during investigation for the purpose of corroborating the statements made by witnesses in court.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was in error to use statements recorded by police under Section 161 Cr.P.C. during the investigation to find corroboration for the statements the witnesses later made in court.
Under Section 162 Cr.P.C., such statements cannot be used by the prosecution for corroboration.
respondent_arguments: The statements recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. were important because they showed that the eyewitnesses had disclosed the appellant's name to the police soon after the FIR was lodged, even though it was not in the FIR itself.
These prior statements to the police confirmed that the witnesses' in-court testimony about hearing the appellant's name was not a belated fabrication.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statement recorded by police under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code during the course of an investigation cannot be used for the purpose of corroborating the testimony of a witness in court. The use of such a statement is restricted by Section 162 of the Code to contradicting a witness.
obiter: The language of Section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code is plain and explicit and admits of no doubt as to its meaning.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court committed a clear legal error by using statements recorded by police under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code to corroborate the testimony of eyewitnesses in court, a practice explicitly prohibited by Section 162. Once this inadmissible evidence was excluded, and considering the absence of a test identification parade and the failure of investigating authorities to arrest the appellant promptly after his name was allegedly disclosed, there was no reliable material left on the record to sustain the conviction, resulting in a grave and substantial injustice.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code, statements made to the police during an investigation cannot be used by the prosecution for the purpose of corroborating the statements made by those witnesses in court. The court noted, 'The language of this section is plain and explicit and it admits of no doubt as to its meaning.'

A conviction must be based on legally admissible evidence, and the court must scrutinize the manner in which the investigation was conducted. After excluding inadmissible evidence, the remaining evidence must be sufficient to prove guilt.
policy_considerations: The High Court's actions in erroneously disregarding the forms of legal process and failing to advert to important and vital aspects of the case caused 'serious prejudice to the appellant.'
The infirmities in the High Court's judgment resulted in a 'prima facie grave and substant.ial injustice' that necessitated setting aside the conviction.
